chunks.text: But don't worry, today we will learn how to speak English at the bank.
This episode is for A1 -level English learners, so I will speak slowly and clearly.
Arriving at the bank When you enter a bank, you may need to talk to the receptionist, wait in line, or take a ticket.
Common phrases.
Hello, I need to open a bank account.
I would like to withdraw some money.
Where is the customer service desk?
Do I need to take a ticket?
How long is the wait?
Example dialogue.
Hello, I need to open a bank account.
Of course, please take a ticket and wait for your number.
Thank you, how long will I have to wait?
Around 15 minutes.
Okay, I'll wait here.
Tip, banks are often busy, especially on Mondays and Fridays.
Try to go during off -peak hours, morning or early afternoon.
Opening a bank account To open a bank account, you may need to provide a passport or ID, proof of address, a bill or rental agreement, an initial deposit.
I would like to open a bank account.
What documents do I need?
What are the different types of accounts?
Is there a minimum balance requirement?
Example dialogue.
Hello, I would like to open a bank account.
Sure, do you have an ID and proof of address?
Yes, here they are.
Thank you.
Would you like a savings account or a checking account?
What's the difference?
Bank clerk.
A savings account is for saving money and earns interest.
A checking account is for daily transactions.
I need a checking account.
Okay, please fill out this form.
Tip.
In the U.S.
and Canada, checking accounts are used for daily spending while savings accounts are for saving money.
Check 3.
Withdrawing and depositing money.
Common phrases.
I would like to withdraw $200.
Can I deposit this check?
What is the daily withdrawal limit?
Can I transfer money to another account?
Example dialogue.
Hello, I would like to withdraw $200.
Do you have your bank card?
Yes, here it is.
Please enter your PIN.
Done.
Thank you.
Tip.
Some ATMs allow cash deposits, but some require you to go inside the bank to deposit money.
Four.
Asking about credit cards and loans.
If you need a credit card or loan, you can ask the bank for information.
Common phrases.
Do you offer credit cards?
What is the interest rate on this loan?
What are the requirements for getting a loan?
Is there an annual fee for this credit card?
Example dialogue.
I'm interested in applying for a credit card.
Sure.
Do you have a job and a bank account with us?
Yes, I do.
Great.
You can apply online or here at the bank.
What's the interest rate?
It's 14 % per year.
Tip.
In some countries, you need a good credit score to get a credit card or loan.
Five.
Exchanging money.
If you are in a foreign country, you may need to exchange currency.
Common phrases.
What is the exchange rate for euros to dollars?
Can I exchange 100 euros to US dollars?
Do you charge a fee for currency exchange?
Example dialogue.
Hello.
I want to exchange 100 euros to US dollars.
The exchange rate today is 1 euro plus 1.1 dollars.
Great.
How much will I get after fees?
You will get 108 dollars.
Thank you.
Tip.
Exchange rates change daily.
So check the rate before you exchange money using N6.
If you don't want to go inside the bank, you can use an ATM automated teller machine.
Common phrases.
How do I use this ATM?
Can I withdraw money from this ATM?
What is the maximum withdrawal amount?
My card is stuck in the ATM.
Can you help me?
Tip.
Some ATMs charge extra fees for withdrawals, especially in airports or convenience stores.
Seven.
Final tips for visiting a bank.
Bring your ID and necessary documents.
Know what service you need before you go.
Ask about fees and policies.
Speak slowly and clearly.
Use polite phrases like please and thank you.
That's the end of today's episode.
I hope you feel more confident speaking English at the bank.
If you enjoyed this episode, please subscribe and share it with your friends.
See you next time.
Good luck.
Thanks for watching.
